That’s why many believe “ the youth vote was key to Democratic Wins in the Midterms .” This sharp turnout increase among an historically under-performing demographic has been building for years. articles.title: Stewards Corner: Laying the Foundation for Change in Your Union
articles.author: Labor Notes Staff
articles.content_excerpt: Revitalizing a local union may require electing new officers with a different vision. But running for office should not be your first step. Successful campaigns for union office usually start by organizing against management first, often years in advance of any eventual run. A group of workers wants to accomplish something—better pay, more control over their conditions on the job, an end to tiered wages or benefits—but their officials, or something about the way their union operates, is in the way. So they begin to change the culture of the union, getting more members involved in building power on the shop floor. articles.title: Do Peasants Hold the Key to Humanity’s Future?
articles.author: Daniel Colligan
articles.content_excerpt: In 1966, the sociologist Teodor Shanin boldly asserted that “peasants are the majority of mankind.” This declaration coincided with the beginning of a decades-long increase in academic focus on the peasantry, which, in addition to its demographic weight, was the driving force of some of the most important political movements of the twentieth century. Classic works such as anthropologist Eric Wolf’s 1969 Peasant Wars of the Twentieth Century chronicled the various ways in which subsistence farmers asserted themselves on the world stage. In the sixty years since Shanin made that declaration, the situation of world agriculture has changed dramatically. articles.title: A History of Taxing the Rich in California
articles.author: Fred Glass
articles.content_excerpt: In the wake of the defeat of Proposition 40, the billionaire tax in California, observers are parsing the loss. The good news is that there were actually two progressive tax ballot measures before the Golden State’s electorate this year, and while we lost Prop 40, we won the other one, Prop 3. This point is key, because it’s not possible to grasp the reasons for the loss of 40 without knowing its intertwined history with Prop 3. Since economic inequality will not be disappearing any time soon, and taxing the rich is an integral aspect of fixing the problem, we need to devise a balance sheet of lessons drawn from these two campaigns to inform the next round. Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see. The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. articles.title: New Colonialism in Latin America
articles.author: Tica Moreno
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. We are living in an era of blatant manipulation, interference, and imperialist aggression against Latin America, and the Brazilian elections were a manifestation of this. At the same time, we are facing both the far right and the empire, with its tech giants. The people’s victory in Brazil had the defense of sovereignty as one of its main pillars: the people affirmed that we are no one’s backyard, understood the implications of Meta’s interference in electoral processes, and more people came to understand the methods of imperialism. There is no doubt that our sovereignty necessarily involves the digital realm, and Lula, having been reelected, is very focused on this agenda.

articles.title: Reject “Electoralism.” Embrace Socialist Electoral Strategy.
articles.author: Elliot Lewis
articles.content_excerpt: In elections this year, 169 (and counting) candidates or ballot initiatives endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) nationally or by its chapters succeeded at city, state, and federal levels. DSA member Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of the largest city in the country, and it seems increasingly possible that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will run for president of the United States in 2028. These exciting developments raise the question of the role of elections in the socialist project. Today some on the Left refer to socialists running for office as “electoralism.” But that term has a specific historical meaning, which much of the radical left has long viewed with disdain. articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Three years into the Gaza genocide, Israel has exposed what its advocates spent more than a century trying to conceal: the violence underlying its claims of victimhood. The story of that concealment stretches back to the beginnings of organized political Zionism. The First Zionist Congress was held in Basel, Switzerland, on August 29–31, 1897. In the decades that followed, the Zionist movement, and eventually Israel, largely managed to hoodwink the world about Palestine and its people. articles.title: The 1973 Athens Polytechnic Uprising Still Matters Today
articles.author: Christos Avramidis
articles.content_excerpt: A military dictatorship had ruled Greece for more than six years when, in November 1973, hundreds of student occupied the Athens Polytechnic, transforming their university into a center of resistance. Thousands of workers, school students, and ordinary citizens soon joined them. On the pillars of the Polytechnic’s central gate, a student painted two messages in large letters: “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.” Within days, on November 17, a military tank would smash through that same gate. Why were young Greeks risking their lives to overthrow the military dictatorship also demanding the withdrawal of the United States and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)? articles.title: Local 256 Secures New Contract, Maintains Union Shop
articles.content_excerpt: Local 256 (MIT-GSU) ratified a new three-year contract with MIT on November 16. They successfully negotiated raises that keep up with inflation — the members will receive a wage increase of 3.5 percent in 2026 (with retroactive pay), 3.25 percent in 2027, and 3.25 percent in 2028. The members gained vacation flexibility, kept their healthcare benefits, and negotiated increased protections for international workers. The local also retained their union shop by organizing an effective strike threat that forced MIT to back down from their demand for an open shop. articles.title: Public Defenders in Massachusetts Can Finally Unionize, But Organizers Say Work Remains
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content_excerpt: Supporters of the “Yes on 2” ballot campaign on election day (Photo courtesy of Mass Defenders United) By: Matt Wolfinger BOSTON – The verdict is in from Bay State voters: public defenders in Massachusetts can finally unionize. Since 1979, public defenders in Massachusetts have been fighting for the right to unionize. After decades of asking elected officials to amend the statute in the state constitution that bars them from unionizing with no success, workers with the Committee for Public Counsel Services (CPCS) put their fate in the hands of voters by securing a spot on the 2026 election ballot. articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A few weeks ago, during a trip to the Philippines, I made my way across congested Manila to Bantayog ng mga Bayani, the memorial in Quezon City to Filipinos who resisted Ferdinand Marcos. The Wall of Remembrance outside, inscribed with the names of those who died resisting, was overrun with grass. I asked one guard where to find the museum, then another, before finding it around a corner. The receptionist asked who I was with. I told her I was a professor and researcher. She indicated to me that there were no tours on Monday and that I’d be free to tour the museum on my own. articles.title: War Budget Is a Path to Spiritual Death
articles.author: Ryan Wentz
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the coming weeks, Congress will be voting on Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion war budget, double the number it was under Biden, which, of course, was already far too high. If passed, the U.S. military budget will be larger than the military budgets of the next 34 countries combined. Thirty-four countries combined. What’s more, while the Pentagon has been audited eight times, not once has it passed.
